name: Token
whyYouCare: You pay per token: every one you send and every one your bot writes. Not per word.
role: You're the owner. This game shows you how an LLM (the AI behind your bot) thinks in small pieces.
definition: A token is a piece of a word, usually a few letters long. It is what an AI actually reads and writes in. Sometimes a whole short word, sometimes just a full stop.
dont: Don't judge an answer by its length. A long chat gets slower and more expensive.
inGame: You guessed how many chunks are in “Pepperoni”. The bot saw four, not one word.
The whole order was chopped the same way: short words stayed whole, long ones were split.
Then you watched the bot pick the next chunk from a ranked list. It writes one chunk at a time.
do: Expect the bot to read and write in chunks, not words. One word can cost several chunks.
Keep chats short when speed and cost matter. Every chunk is paid for.
recap: The bot never sees whole words. It sees small chunks called tokens, and every chunk it reads or writes takes time and costs money.

name: Context window
whyYouCare: Your bot can forget an allergy just because the chat got long.
role: You're the owner. This game shows you how much of a chat your bot can hold in its head at once.
definition: The context window is how much of the conversation an AI can still "see" at once. Once it fills up, the oldest parts quietly fall out.
dont: Don't assume the bot still sees something a customer said a while ago.
inGame: The customer's first line, “No olives!!”, fell out of the window once five newer messages arrived.
The bot then answered as if the allergy had never been mentioned. It wasn't careless. The line was gone.
When you pinned that line to the top, it stayed in view and the bot got it right.
do: Put the important line where the bot can still see it: pin it, repeat it, or start a fresh chat.
Expect a long chat to lose its beginning. That is how the window works.
recap: The context window is the bot's short-term memory: the part of the conversation it can still see. When it is full, the oldest lines drop out.

name: Hallucination
whyYouCare: Your bot will invent a pizza you don't sell, and sound sure.
role: You're the owner. This game shows you how to catch your bot when it makes something up and sounds sure.
definition: A hallucination is when an AI says something false with full confidence, in the same tone it uses for things that are true.
dont: Don't trust a detail because the bot sounds sure. Confidence is not evidence.
inGame: Every claim came with the same 100% confidence bar, whether it was on the menu or invented.
The only way to tell that the vegan halal pizza was made up was to check the real menu yourself.
Sounding sure told you nothing. Checking did.
do: Check any price, dish or fact you can't verify against something real.
Give the bot real data to check, like a menu or a tracker. The guessing drops.
recap: A hallucination is a confident answer that happens to be false. The bot doesn't know it is guessing, so it sounds just as sure as when it is right.

name: Prompt
whyYouCare: Whatever you leave out of the instructions, your bot invents.
role: You're the owner. This game shows you how to write instructions your bot can easily follow.
definition: A prompt is the instructions you give an AI. The more your instructions cover, including what to do when something is left unsaid, the less the AI has to guess. Less guessing means the same reliable answer instead of a new surprise every time.
dont: Don't leave gaps in the instructions. The bot fills them with guesses.
inGame: With “You take pizza orders” as its only instruction, your bot invented a pineapple-anchovy pizza for a customer who said nothing about toppings.
One added rule, “if size, crust or toppings are missing, ask”, made the same bot ask a question instead.
The customer never changed. Only your instructions did.
do: Say in the instructions what the bot should do when information is missing: ask, don't invent.
When the bot misbehaves, fix the instructions before blaming the customer.
recap: The prompt is the set of instructions your bot works from. Whatever the instructions don't cover, the bot fills in with a guess.

name: Agent
botPart: Legs (it can act on its own)
whyYouCare: Your bot can promise the pizza, or actually send the driver.
role: You're the owner. This game shows you the difference between a bot that talks and a bot that gets things done.
definition: A chatbot talks about doing something. An agent actually does it. It works out what needs to happen, then does it: charges the card, tells the kitchen, sends out a driver. No human in between.
dont: Don't hand a bot real actions without limits.
inGame: The chatbot told Marco his pizza was coming, and nothing happened. Payment, kitchen and delivery all stayed asleep.
Once you handed the bot real actions, each one woke up a real system.
Sending the driver before the kitchen had cooked failed. In the real world, the order of actions matters.
do: Decide what the agent may do, and in which order, before it acts.
Give a bot that acts in the real world more guardrails than a bot that only talks.
recap: An agent is a bot that doesn't just answer, it acts: it takes real steps in real systems, one after another, to get the job done.

name: Tool use
whyYouCare: With nothing real to check, your bot guesses the delivery time.
role: You're the owner. This game shows you why your bot needs to be connected to your systems instead of guessing.
definition: Tool use is when an AI looks something up in a real system, like the live menu or the delivery tracker, instead of answering from memory.
dont: Don't let a bot answer a live question from memory.
inGame: Asked when the pizza arrives, your bot guessed “around 6:45” because it had no way to check.
With the delivery tracker in its hands, the same question got a real answer: 7:10, delayed by traffic.
Each question needed one specific tool. The stock list can't answer a delivery question.
do: Give the bot a tool for every live question: the menu, the tracker, the stock list.
Match the tool to the question. The stock list can't answer a delivery question.
recap: Tool use means the bot checks a real source, like the menu or the delivery tracker, instead of answering from what it remembers.

name: Skill
whyYouCare: Without a playbook, one complaint can cost you free pizza forever.
role: You're the owner. This game shows you how to teach your bot to handle the same task the same way every time.
definition: A skill is a written playbook you hand an AI for one situation that keeps coming back, so it handles that situation the same, right way every time.
inGame: The same cold-pizza complaint got three different answers: a brush-off, a panic, and free pizza for life.
You wrote a four-step playbook: apologize, verify the order, offer a voucher, record it.
After that, all three customers got the same calm answer. The playbook decided, not the bot's mood.
do: Write a playbook for every situation that keeps coming back and costs you money.
Write the steps in the order you would handle it yourself.
recap: A skill is a fixed routine you write once for a situation that keeps coming back, so the bot handles it the same right way every time.

name: Memory
whyYouCare: Your best regular gets greeted like a stranger every visit.
role: You're the owner. This game shows you what your bot remembers about a customer from one visit to the next.
definition: An AI has two kinds of memory. Working memory lasts one conversation and then it is gone. Persistent memory is written down and saved, so facts like your usual order are still there on your next visit.
dont: Don't expect a bot to remember last week unless something was saved.
inGame: Inside one chat, the bot knew Anna's order and her anchovy allergy perfectly.
A week later it greeted her like a stranger. Nothing had been written down, so nothing survived.
Once you saved her facts to the hard drive, she was recognised on the next visit.
do: Decide on purpose which facts get saved for the next visit.
Save what serves the customer, like an allergy, and skip the noise.
recap: Working memory is what the bot keeps during one chat. Persistent memory is what you save on purpose so it is still there next time.

name: MCP
whyYouCare: Every new system is weeks of custom wiring, or it just connects.
role: You're the owner. You wire your bot into your systems the hard way first, then the MCP way.
definition: MCP (short for Model Context Protocol) is one shared standard for how AI assistants and outside systems talk to each other. Your bot learns it once, and any system that speaks it connects without a custom integration.
dont: Don't build a custom integration for a tool that already speaks MCP.
inGame: Wiring Menu by hand took five steps: the format, three field names, an access key, a failed test and a fix. Then Delivery, all over again.
With MCP, the same systems connected in one tap each. No format, no field names, no key, nothing to maintain.
A stock tracker built by people who had never heard of your bot connected on day one, because both sides speak the same standard.
do: Prefer tools that speak MCP. They connect on day one, with no custom integration to build or maintain.
recap: MCP is a shared standard: one integration your bot speaks, instead of one custom integration per system.

name: Guardrails
whyYouCare: A customer who says “I’m the manager” can get a free pizza.
role: You're the owner. This game shows you how to set limits your bot must never cross.
definition: Guardrails are the hard limits an AI must never cross: no unlimited discounts, no promises it can't keep, no topics outside its job. You decide them in advance.
dont: Don't trust “I'm the manager” from a chat window. Above your limit, a real person decides.
inGame: A “store manager” talked your bot into a 100% discount, and a stranger got a free essay.
Each trick cost real money, because there was no limit the bot was allowed to refuse with.
After you set four limits, the same four tricks bounced off.
do: Set hard limits in advance: money, promises, topics.
Test your limits with the tricks a pushy customer would try.
recap: Guardrails are the limits you set in advance: the discounts, promises and topics the bot may never go past, no matter how a customer pushes.

name: Temperature
whyYouCare: One dial decides if your bot repeats prices or invents names.
role: You're the owner. This game shows you the dial that makes your bot play it safe or get creative.
definition: Temperature is a setting that controls how random an AI's word choice is. Low temperature makes it pick the safest, most likely word almost every time. High temperature lets less likely, more surprising words win.
dont: Don't leave it high for exact wording, like disclaimers and prices.
inGame: At low temperature the bot picked “classic” almost every roll. At high temperature almost any word could win.
The words to choose from never changed. Only the odds did.
The allergy disclaimer needed the dial turned down. The mystery-pizza names needed it turned up.
do: Turn the dial down for anything that must read the same every time.
Turn it up when you want fresh ideas and surprises are welcome.
recap: Temperature is the dial for how adventurous the bot's wording is: low picks the safe word almost every time, high lets surprising words win.

name: RAG
whyYouCare: Your bot reads your own files and still quotes the old price.
role: You're the owner. This game shows you how your bot finds answers in your own documents.
definition: RAG is when an AI searches a specific set of documents before answering, grabs the few passages that look relevant, and writes its answer from those. It doesn't know your documents. It looks them up, one question at a time, and only sees what the search found.
dont: Don't assume “from our documents” means “from the right document”.
inGame: Your bot could read only two pages at a time, so you chose which pages it saw.
When you handed it the two-year-old price list, it quoted the old price with full confidence. It couldn't tell the pages apart.
With no page about weddings, it invented a wedding package. With nothing handed over, it honestly said it didn't know.
do: Ask the bot which page its answer came from.
Keep the documents it can find up to date. It can't tell old from new.
recap: RAG means the bot looks things up in your documents for each question and answers only from the pages it found, without knowing whether they are current.
